title: Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence: founding scene and field-naming conjecture
summary: Dartmouth 1956 is promoted as the first bounded field-founding scene record. The record does not claim that AI was born from one place alone; it encodes a source-backed scene where the term artificial intelligence, a field-building proposal, and early institutional memory converged around a conjecture that intelligence could be precisely described and simulated by machines.

status_history.note: The seed document listed the Dartmouth Workshop 1956 among dense science/computing scenes worth mapping.
Promoted using two Dartmouth institutional sources; full archival proposal and attendee list still require extraction.

scope_cautions: A field-founding scene is not a monocausal origin story.
The proposal conjecture is encoded as a historically important programmatic claim, not as a fact that was already established.
Scene records must separate who attended, who organized, who coined terminology, and what later influence can be shown.
type_payload.why_it_matters_for_missing_half: It gives the cube an upstream promise-node for later negative-result/program-audit records such as ALPAC and Lighthill without turning those audits into anti-AI hindsight.

links.note: Machine translation was one of the early computational-language promises that later received program-audit scrutiny.
Lighthill is encoded as a later evaluator/anti-genealogy scene in AI, not as a direct response solely to Dartmouth.

handling_notes: Avoid great-man-only framing; later revisions should add women, translators, programmers, funders, laboratories, and non-US/non-UK lineages.
Do not use downstream disappointments to mock early researchers; encode promise, uncertainty, evidence, and later correction separately.
